summary: Proposes a strawman position on goals and approaches for the IETF, IESG, and IAB on two related topics: supporting multiple protocols in the Internet and choosing a next-generation Internet Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet was deciding whether to run many languages at once and what the next IP should be. This paper offers a rough plan.

subtitle: The IAB's strawman position on protocol standardization and coexistence

tldr.problem: The Internet faced growing pressure to support multiple protocol suites (like OSI and IPX) alongside TCP/IP, and the IETF needed to decide whether to pursue a single next-generation IP or allow multiple competing versions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes a framework where the IETF maintains TCP/IP as its primary focus, selects a single next-generation Internet protocol, and develops mechanisms for interoperability with other protocol suites where necessary, rather than treating all protocols equally.
tldr.outcome: This position became influential in the IETF's eventual adoption of IPv6 as the single next-generation Internet protocol and shaped how the community approaches protocol evolution.

today: RFC 1560 is an Informational RFC presenting the IAB's strawman position in 1993. The community largely adopted its recommendations: TCP/IP remained the primary suite, IPv6 was selected as the next-generation Internet protocol, and the IETF developed transition mechanisms (dual-stack, tunneling) for the IPv4 to IPv6 transition. It is a historical record of how the Internet community chose to manage protocol evolution.

sections.title: The Multiprotocol Challenge
sections.content:
By 1993, the Internet faced a strategic question: should it embrace multiple protocol suites, or maintain focus on a single suite (TCP/IP)? The document was prepared by Barry Leiner and Yakov Rekhter on behalf of the Internet Architecture Board to propose a strawman position—a starting point for discussion rather than a final recommendation.

The core tension is pragmatic: in reality, multiple protocol stacks exist and will continue to exist (IPv6 vs. IPv4, OSI protocols, IPX/SPX, SNA). However, the Internet's strength derives from having a single common virtual network layer (IP) that enables ubiquitous communication and a large market for applications. The question is whether to preserve that unity or accommodate fragmentation.
sections.plainLanguage: In the early 1990s, the Internet had to decide: should it support many different networking languages at once, or stick with one main language?

sections.title: How Protocols Evolve and Coexist
sections.content:
The RFC describes a dynamic model of multiprotocol integration where a primary protocol suite (TCP/IP) interacts with other suites through two mechanisms. Interoperability allows systems using different protocols to communicate, for example by translating messages at application layers. Resource sharing allows different protocol suites to use the same physical links and switching infrastructure without interfering.

Both mechanisms are difficult and often cause unanticipated interactions. A protocol suite that aggressively consumes bandwidth may starve others if they use different congestion control strategies. Interoperability is hard when protocols have different semantic models. To manage these challenges, the primary protocol suite (TCP/IP) must evolve while remaining stable, a process called harmonization—communities discuss and align their approaches, leading to gradual convergence.

Within a single protocol suite, evolution also creates temporary multiplicity: IPv4 and IPv6 will coexist for years, requiring transition mechanisms. The RFC argues this same evolutionary framework applies whether dealing with protocol suites or versions.
sections.plainLanguage: When different computer languages try to coexist, they need translators and agreed-upon shared resources. Over time, through talking and testing, the community can gradually move toward one language.

sections.title: What the IETF/IESG/IAB Should Do
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that the IETF/IESG/IAB adopt a dual strategy. First, act as a force for convergence on a single primary protocol suite (TCP/IP) and evolution of that suite to meet changing needs. This preserves the benefits of a unified network layer and enables applications to rely on common infrastructure.

Second, develop and maintain mechanisms for interoperability and resource sharing with other protocol suites where they exist. This pragmatically acknowledges that OSI, IPX, and other stacks have communities of users and legacy deployments that cannot disappear overnight. The goal is to minimize negative impact on TCP/IP while allowing coexistence.

The RFC notes that communities working on other protocol suites have a complementary perspective; they too must balance their own evolution with interoperability. The IETF's role is to ensure TCP/IP succeeds while facilitating compatibility.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet community should focus its energy on making TCP/IP better and more consistent, but also learn to translate messages when it meets other languages.

sections.title: Why a Single Internet Protocol Layer Matters
sections.content:
The RFC argues that having a single Internet protocol (like IP) is not merely a convenience but essential to the Internet's success. A common network layer creates a ubiquitous communication infrastructure, which in turn allows end users—not network operators—to choose their applications. If multiple incompatible Internet protocols existed, users would need to know which applications work on which protocol, or choose a protocol based on what applications they need, rather than on their actual communication requirements.

A common infrastructure also creates a large marketplace for application developers, who can build and deploy applications knowing they will run on the universal network service. This was crucial to the explosion of application diversity on the Internet.

Alternatives, such as running different transport protocols over the same Internet protocol, or achieving interoperability via common application services, do not provide the same benefits. Therefore, the community should select and commit to a single next-generation Internet protocol (IPng) and develop mechanisms to ease the transition from IPv4, rather than allowing multiple versions to compete indefinitely.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone speaks one language (IP), it is easy to build things on top of it. If everyone speaks different languages, builders do not know which one to support.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC concludes that the IETF/IESG/IAB should maintain its historical role as a force for convergence by:

Maintaining focus on TCP/IP. Continue developing the TCP/IP protocol suite as the primary platform for Internet evolution, rather than giving equal weight to other protocol families.

Selecting a single next-generation Internet protocol. Choose one IPng candidate and develop a migration path from IPv4. Do not allow the market to decide this; the Internet layer is not the right place for competition among incompatible versions.

Exploring mechanisms for interoperability. While preserving the primacy of TCP/IP, develop techniques for sharing resources and achieving interoperability with other protocol suites to minimize disruption during transition periods.
sections.plainLanguage: Stick with TCP/IP as the main language, pick one new version (IPv6) and build a translator to move from the old version, but do not try to support everything at once.

references.text: Clark, D., Chapin, L., Cerf, V., Braden, R., and R. Hobby, "Towards the Future Internet Architecture", RFC 1287, MIT, BBN, CNRI, ISI, UC Davis, December 1991.
